text: Every gate you've met so far in this chapter is fixed — X, Y, Z, H, S, and T each have one specific matrix and nothing adjustable. Rotation gates break that pattern: Rx, Ry, and Rz are entire continuous families, parameterized by an angle theta, and the fixed gates you already know turn out to be special cases hiding inside them.

Each rotation gate rotates the qubit's state around one axis of the Bloch sphere by an angle theta. Ry's matrix is entirely real: cosine theta-over-2, negative sine theta-over-2, sine theta-over-2, cosine theta-over-2. Rx and Rz look similar but carry imaginary entries. Notice theta-over-2, not theta, inside every entry — a quirk tied to qubits being spin-one-half systems.

Computing Ry of pi-over-2 on ket-zero gives 0.7071, 0.7071 — numerically identical to H on ket-zero. Tempting to call them the same gate. But Ry of pi-over-2 on ket-one gives negative 0.7071, 0.7071, which is the negative of H on ket-one. Squaring gives identical probabilities either way, but as state vectors they're genuinely different. The lesson: two gates agreeing on one basis vector's output doesn't mean they're the same gate — you have to check the full matrix.

Set theta to pi in Rx and compare to X: Rx of pi comes out to negative i times the X matrix exactly. Rz of pi comes out to negative i times the Z matrix exactly. A global phase like that negative i multiplies the entire state vector uniformly and is never detectable by any measurement — different from the relative phase you saw earlier, which can become observable through interference. So Rx and Rz, at the right angle, reproduce every fixed gate you've learned, up to a global phase, and theta reaches everything in between — exactly the knob real quantum hardware drives with a pulse.
Next lesson is practice: chaining these gates together and computing exact numbers at every step, building the habit of never assuming how a multi-gate sequence turns out.
